paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Where have we been? Gina, I’m not sure who’s going to… Okay, thank you. I don’t have anyone yet, but if someone decides to join, we can.

All right. Questions? And Nick lied to you. I did not say, “Give me the hardest questions.” But you can give me hard questions. I might just not be able to answer them. You can just open your microphones or type them in.
You can turn on your cameras too. It’s actually helpful for me to see your beautiful faces. I’m going to read Olga’s question first and then decide if I’m going to answer it.

chapters.title: Creating someone who can remove bad seeds

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I like Olga’s question. Olga asked: the idea is that we can plant seeds to create anything, so can you create someone or something to take away all of our bad seeds?
I think where this question is coming from is: if a Buddha had the power, if an enlightened being had the power to take away our suffering—okay, let me ask a different question.
If a Buddha were omnipotent, if there were a being who was infinitely compassionate and infinitely powerful, who could do anything, what proves to us that they’re not infinitely powerful?

paragraphs.speaker: Christina
paragraphs.text: They would have taken everyone out of *samsara* immediately if they were able to.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: That’s correct. If they had infinite compassion and they had the power to take away your suffering, what’s the proof that they’re not infinitely powerful? We’re still suffering.
The proof is that because we’re still suffering, if they were able to do it, they would do it. But somehow they haven’t.

So Olga’s question is interesting. Why can’t we just plant the seeds to create someone or something outside of us who can take away our suffering? Or how do we do that? I’ll let you know, Olga, when I figure it out.

But what I can say is: when your practice gets really good, when you start keeping your morality and your ethics really well, and you have the intention to help other people, really cool stuff starts happening.

If you’re about to do something wrong, and your practice is really good, something may happen. For example, I used to do this thing where I would lie just a little bit. We call them white lies. Little white lies would come out of my mouth. They wouldn’t really hurt anyone, but they were just little tiny lies.

Then I started discovering that before I would tell a little lie, I would start to feel a little bit of *prana* collecting in my throat, right about here. I started getting this awareness that any time I was about to lie, I would feel it first.

At first I would feel it and then I would not be able to stop it. The train wreck was already happening. Then I got to the point where I would notice it and think, “Oh, I shouldn’t say that,” but the train wreck would happen anyway.

Now it’s mostly to the point where I feel it and I go, “Why do I feel compelled to not tell the truth?” Then I just keep my mouth shut. Usually it’s about protecting myself so people don’t think I’m an idiot, or that I didn’t fulfill the promise I made, or something like that.

Then something cool started happening for me. If I’m about to do something I shouldn’t do, something that’s going to create a bad karma, people around me stop me from doing it. Someone will interrupt me. Then I’ll have this observation: “Oh, that person—my karma ripened to stop me from doing something bad.”

I remember a time, years ago, when I was still working corporate jobs and taking a lot of time off to go to Diamond Mountain. I didn’t really tell my boss I was going. I had planned to work from home, work remotely, and then I realized it was too busy. I thought, “Dang, I have to make an excuse.”

I was actually with Geshe Michael. I picked up my phone to text, “Hey guys, I’m not feeling that well today…” I was making up some reason why I couldn’t work. As I started typing it, Geshe Michael, from the other side of the room, said, “Hey Tim, can you get me some Cheerios?”

I put my phone down, got up, and got some Cheerios. Cheerios is a breakfast cereal. I made Geshe-la some breakfast. I brought him the breakfast, and I thought, “Oh, look, I get to make Geshe Michael breakfast. I’m awesome.”
Then I sat back down and realized that he had interrupted me having an affliction. He stopped me from lying to my boss.

So in a way, I would say that yes, it’s possible to create someone who can help take away your suffering, but it’s not like they can pull it out of you. It’s not like they can just rip those bad seeds out. My karma ripened so I could see people in my life protecting me.

That comes from protecting others, taking care of other people, making sure they’re doing the right things, helping them in gentle ways. Don’t go around and start being a jerk: “You’re not keeping your vows, Gina. You’re breaking your Vajrayana vows.” Don’t do that to people. Don’t karma-blame other people.
But help other people be better people. Help them be kinder people. Help them do nicer things.

My co-managers had some problem with their house, and they discovered they could get insurance money if they had stayed at a hotel while they were having problems at their house. They said, “Can I just print out a reservation and send it to them to get the money?”
I said, “Well, you could do that. I’ll even tell you how to do it. But I wouldn’t do it. That’s insurance fraud. You didn’t stay in the hotel.” I said, “You can do what you want.”

So help other people, Olga. Be kinder. Help them do the right thing, but don’t be a jerk about it. Don’t be mean to other people when you think they’re doing the wrong thing. Don’t be tight. Don’t think you’re right. Just gently help them.

Then weird stuff happens. Geshe Michael will ask you to get Cheerios when you’re about to have an affliction. The punchline to that story is: I still lied to my boss. I feel bad about it. This was years ago. But at least he tried, and at least I could celebrate that.
